input: Compare SatisFix's pass@1 gains on DeepSWE vs. SWE-bench Pro hard subset, and its margin over the best baseline on DeepSWE.
expected_output: SatisFix raises the base agent's pass@1 by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, so the gain is about 1.97 points larger on the SWE-bench Pro hard subset. On DeepSWE, it also outperforms the best self-correction baseline by 3.98%. The context does not give a baseline margin for SWE-bench Pro.

input: Compare original vs reference-grouped evaluation: how do memory effect, copy baseline RC, and leakage differ?
expected_output: Original split: memory improved reference conformity (RC) by 0.015 [0.004, 0.025] over no-memory, but an audit showed 264 of 367 held-out units (72%) shared a PostgreSQL reference with training; on the 103 leak-free units the memory effect fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011]. The nearest-target copy baseline scored RC 0.222, beating all LLM systems (at most 0.163). Reference-grouped split: copying dropped to 0.119, and a rerun on 374 units in 118 independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect (0.005 [-0.003, 0.017]) and no policy effect. So grouping reduced leakage-driven copying and showed the original memory gain mostly reflected reference reuse rather than learning.

input: In Laya, which confidence field is calibrated by temperature scaling, and how does it differ from entropy-based confidence for choice/score vs two-option noul questions?
expected_output: Temperature scaling is fitted for answer_confidence, which is max(p), the probability mass on the reported answer. The separate field called confidence is different for choice and score questions: it is a normalised entropy, 1 - H(p)/log k, which measures how concentrated the whole distribution is rather than the probability of the chosen answer. For two-option noul questions the two fields coincide.

input: How does Rasoi's versioned visual diff meet DG1-DG3 and help 12 developers check scope, spot restructuring, and gain evaluation confidence in its week-long study?
expected_output: DG1: Rasoi uses versioned visual maps, with each session made of multiple comparable snapshots, so developers see how architecture changes across agent iterations rather than only the current state. DG2: it supports movement between high-level architectural overviews and code-level detail across abstraction levels, so developers can re-orient quickly and still trace bugs or verify components. DG3 aims to preserve important codebase details without cluttering the visualization, though the context doesn't explain how this is implemented. In the week-long study with 12 developers on their own codebases, visual diffs helped them see whether changes stayed within scope, notice unexpected restructuring, and understand how modified parts related to the whole system. The findings suggest the tool's value lies less in making developers trust the agent and more in helping them feel confident in their own evaluation of agent-made changes.

input: Compare access gaps versus reasoning errors in the agent's concurrency incidents: how often did each occur, and were hypotheses evidence-consistent or fabrications?
expected_output: Access gaps were the more pervasive problem: they were present in all five concurrency-dependent incidents, alone in one and combined with a reasoning error in the other four. Reasoning errors (anchoring on an early cause, incomplete exploration of the configuration, or misreading the code's transaction semantics) therefore occurred in four of the five, never without an access gap. The three non-concurrency incidents needed nothing beyond the agent's existing access. As for the hypotheses, the wrong ones were evidence-consistent, meaning they agreed with everything the agent had observed, and were not fabrications.

input: If accuracy-oriented configs raised shots 10x but top-state probability stayed flat, why might the proxy metric, not the config, be at fault?
expected_output: Because top-state probability measures sampling concentration, not true fidelity, energy error, approximation ratio, or task accuracy. Shots change sampling variance but not the underlying quantum state's accuracy, so 10x more shots wouldn't necessarily raise it. In variational algorithm simulations, random parameters add extra variability. The paper therefore treats the null result as a limitation of the proxy metric, not proof that accuracy-oriented configurations can't improve task quality.

input: ORBIT ingestion: what are the passage size, embedding model, and vector store, and why do passages keep sources?
expected_output: ORBIT splits the cleaned corpus into sentence-aware passages of about 500 characters with small overlap, encodes them with gemini-embedding-001 (3,072 dimensions), and indexes them in a Postgres vector store. Each passage keeps its source so that items keep their context, and the identifiers of the chosen passages are stored with the item for later checking.

input: Compare industry involvement and academia-only shares in LLM-based vs non-LLM-based ICSE Research-track papers, 2023-2026.
expected_output: Across 2023-2026 ICSE Research-track papers, industry involvement is higher in LLM-based work (23.4%) than in non-LLM-based work (16.9%). Academia-only papers make up a smaller share of LLM-based papers (63.4%) than of non-LLM-based papers (70.9%).

input: How does CoReMem differ from SWE-MeM, ReasoningBank, and MemOp in carrying repo state and memory, and optimizing for next-task gain?
expected_output: Per Figure 2, CoReMem is the only setting where both repo state and memory carry to unseen future tasks, with memory valued and optimized for gain on the next task. SWE-MeM (context compaction) stays within one task, so nothing carries over. ReasoningBank (across repositories) carries only general insights via an experience bank between independent tasks. MemOp (same repo, reset) carries memory but resets the repository, handing over the gold fix, and is optimized for gain on the same task rather than the next one.

input: If AskALCF finds R false and C true for a failed query, which component gets blamed? What if both are false?
expected_output: If R is false and C is true, the failure is assigned to retrieval: the corpus contains the answer, but the top-k passages returned in production were insufficient. If both R and C are false, the failure is assigned to knowledge, because the corpus lacks sufficient documentation.

input: Which papers study memory for coding or migration agents, and what did they find about whether memory actually helps?
expected_output: Two papers. The Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration study (2611.16143) found that persistent experience memory improved reference conformity by only 0.015 over a no-memory baseline, and the effect almost vanished (0.002) on leak-free units; a rerun on independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect. CoReMem (2611.17316) builds a cost-internalizing memory of repository anchors for successive coding tasks and raised a 27B actor's resolve rate on ChainSWE from 21.0% to 25.7% with 17% fewer steps.

input: Which benchmarks are used to evaluate coding agents on software issue resolution, and what improvements did the proposed methods report on them?
expected_output: SatisFix (2611.16289) is evaluated on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Pro: it improves the base agent's pass@1 by 5.09% on average on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and beats the best self-correction baseline on DeepSWE by 3.98%. CoReMem (2611.17316) is evaluated on ChainSWE, where it raises the resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7% with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer tokens.

input: What evaluation pitfalls do papers report when benchmarking LLM-based systems?
expected_output: ORBIT (2611.15718) found template defects in about a tenth of generated items, that models judging their own answers accepted many answers to defective items (so one independent judge is used), and that word overlap with the question picks the correct multiple-choice option more than half the time. The migration-agent study (2611.16143) found reference leakage: 72% of held-out units shared a reference with training, and a model-free nearest-target copy baseline (RC 0.222) beat all LLM systems (at most 0.163); it derives six evaluation rules to separate learning from leakage and copying.

input: What do the papers say about human oversight of AI coding agents?
expected_output: Rasoi (2611.16293) shows visual architecture diffs help developers check that agent changes stay in scope and spot unexpected restructuring; in a week-long study with 12 developers, oversight tools mattered more for developers' confidence in their own evaluation than for trusting the agent. The database-debugging study (2611.17304) found Claude Code repeatedly announced and walked back wrong causes, mainly because it lacked access to production state, and proposes a forensics layer. The migration study (2611.16143) reports that a human-gated fix cycle raised demonstrably correct units from 98/216 to 167/224.

input: Which papers address IT operations or production support, and what are their main contributions?
expected_output: ORBIT (2611.15718) is an evidence-grounded benchmark of ITOps questions (multiple-choice, open-ended, troubleshooting) showing models handle most multiple-choice items but only a minority of troubleshooting items. AskALCF (2611.15700) is a self-improving agentic pipeline for HPC user support that attributes failures to components and reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2% across 2,174 support turns. The database-debugging study (2611.17304) analyzes an agent diagnosing eight production database incidents and finds missing access to production state was the main bottleneck.
